claim: Cigarette smoking is a well-known risk factor inducing the development and progression of various diseases.
source: Cigarette smoking is a well-known risk factor inducing the development and progression of various diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement presented in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence, but it represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Nicotine (NIC) is the major constituent of cigarette smoke.
source: Nicotine (NIC) is the major constituent of cigarette smoke.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the composition of cigarette smoke.

claim: NIC increases the abundance and proliferative activity of murine intestinal stem cells (ISCs) in vivo and ex vivo.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that NIC increases the abundance and proliferative activity of murine intestinal stem cells (ISCs) in vivo and ex vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2, including Ki67 staining, Olfm4 staining, and organoid formation assays.

claim: NIC induces Yes-associated protein (YAP)/Transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ) and Notch signaling in ISCs via α7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR) and protein kinase C (PKC) activation.
source: Moreover, NIC induces Yes-associated protein (YAP) /Transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ) and Notch signaling in ISCs via α7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR) and protein kinase C (PKC) activation; this effect was not detected in Paneth cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 3, 4, and 5, including receptor antagonist studies, immunoblotting, and qPCR analyses.

claim: The effect of NIC on ISCs was not detected in Paneth cells.
source: Moreover, NIC induces Yes-associated protein (YAP) /Transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ) and Notch signaling in ISCs via α7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR) and protein kinase C (PKC) activation; this effect was not detected in Paneth cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2, 3, and 4 showing differential responses between ISCs and Paneth cells.

claim: The inhibition of Notch signaling by dibenzazepine (DBZ) nullified the effects of NIC on ISCs.
source: The inhibition of Notch signaling by dibenzazepine (DBZ) nullified the effects of NIC on ISCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6 showing that DBZ treatment prevents NIC-induced ISC expansion.

claim: NIC enhances in vivo tumor formation from ISCs after loss of the tumor suppressor gene Apc.
source: NIC enhances in vivo tumor formation from ISCs after loss of the tumor suppressor gene Apc, DBZ inhibited NIC-induced tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7 using Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice showing increased polyp formation in NIC-treated mice.

claim: DBZ inhibited NIC-induced tumor growth.
source: NIC enhances in vivo tumor formation from ISCs after loss of the tumor suppressor gene Apc, DBZ inhibited NIC-induced tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7E and F showing that DBZ treatment reduces polyp formation in NIC-treated Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice.

claim: Abnormal stem cell functions are significantly associated with age-related organ dysfunction and carcinogenesis.
source: Abnormal stem cell functions are significantly associated with age-related organ dysfunction and carcinogenesis (Adams et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adams et al., 2015.

claim: Intestinal epithelial turnover is sustained by intestinal stem cells (ISCs) and adjacent Paneth cells.
source: Intestinal epithelial turnover is sustained by intestinal stem cells (ISCs) and adjacent Paneth cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about intestinal homeostasis.

claim: Paneth cells constitute the niche for ISCs that reside at the bottom of the crypts.
source: Paneth cells constitute the niche for ISCs that reside at the bottom of the crypts.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the intestinal stem cell niche.

claim: Most of the ISCs are leucine-rich repeat-containing G-protein-coupled receptor 5 (Lgr5) +ones that regulate intestinal homeostasis in response to dietary signals.
source: Most of the ISCs are leucine-rich repeat-containing G-protein-coupled receptor 5 (Lgr5) +ones that regulate intestinal homeostasis in response to dietary signals (Igarashi and Guarente, 2016; Yilmaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Igarashi and Guarente, 2016 and Yilmaz et al., 2012.

claim: In the intestine, Lgr5 +ISCs are possibly the origin of precancerous adenomas.
source: In the intestine, Lgr5 +ISCs are possibly the origin of precancerous adenomas (Barker et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barker et al., 2009.

claim: Long-term high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity enhances the self-renewal potential of ISC and promotes in vivo formation of tumors via the induction of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta in ISCs.
source: For instance, long-term high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity enhances the self-renewal potential of ISC and promotes in vivo formation of tumors via the induction of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta in ISCs (Beyaz et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beyaz et al., 2016.

claim: Cigarette smoking has emerged as a potential major risk factor associated with colon cancer, along with metabolic risk factors such as diet and obesity.
source: Moreover, cigarette smoking has emerged as a potential major risk factor associated with colon cancer, along with metabolic risk factors such as diet and obesity.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Cigarette smoking is significantly associated with colon cancer and mortality in humans.
source: Previous studies indicate that cigarette smoking is significantly associated with colon cancer and mortality in humans (Botteri et al., 2008) and animal models (Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Botteri et al., 2008.

claim: Cigarette smoking is significantly associated with colon cancer and mortality in animal models.
source: Previous studies indicate that cigarette smoking is significantly associated with colon cancer and mortality in humans (Botteri et al., 2008) and animal models (Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2008.

claim: Nicotine (NIC) derivatives 4-(methylnitrosamino)–1-(3-pyridyl)–1-butanone (NNK) and N'-nitrosonornicotine (NNN) are highly carcinogenic.
source: Cigarette smoke contains a wide range of compounds that are harmful to human health; nicotine (NIC) derivatives 4-(methylnitrosamino)–1-(3-pyridyl)–1-butanone (NNK) and N'-nitrosonornicotine (NNN) are highly carcinogenic (Brunnemann and Hoffmann, 1991; Schuller et al., 1995), which can induce mutations in tumor suppressive genes like Rasa, Trp53, and Rb (Sekido et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brunnemann and Hoffmann, 1991 and Schuller et al., 1995.

claim: NNK and NNN can induce mutations in tumor suppressive genes like Rasa, Trp53, and Rb.
source: Cigarette smoke contains a wide range of compounds that are harmful to human health; nicotine (NIC) derivatives 4-(methylnitrosamino)–1-(3-pyridyl)–1-butanone (NNK) and N'-nitrosonornicotine (NNN) are highly carcinogenic (Brunnemann and Hoffmann, 1991; Schuller et al., 1995), which can induce mutations in tumor suppressive genes like Rasa, Trp53, and Rb (Sekido et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sekido et al., 2003.

claim: NIC itself, the addictive component in cigarette smoke, is generally considered to have a limited ability to initiate cancer.
source: Although NIC itself, the addictive component in cigarette smoke, is generally considered to have a limited ability to initiate cancer, it can stimulate several effects crucial for cancer development independently (Schaal and Chellappan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schaal and Chellappan, 2014.

claim: NIC can stimulate several effects crucial for cancer development independently.
source: Although NIC itself, the addictive component in cigarette smoke, is generally considered to have a limited ability to initiate cancer, it can stimulate several effects crucial for cancer development independently (Schaal and Chellappan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schaal and Chellappan, 2014.

claim: NIC exposure decreased villus length without affecting crypt size.
source: Histological analyses of the small intestine in C57BL/6 mice treated with 200 μg/ml NIC (which emulates active smoking) revealed that NIC exposure decreased villus length without affecting crypt size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which was consistent with NIC-induced decrease in the number of differentiated cells, including absorptive enterocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) or chromogranin A+enteroendocrine cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), in the gut.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NIC-induced decrease in the number of differentiated cells, including absorptive enterocytes.
source: Histological analyses of the small intestine in C57BL/6 mice treated with 200 μg/ml NIC (which emulates active smoking) revealed that NIC exposure decreased villus length without affecting crypt size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which was consistent with NIC-induced decrease in the number of differentiated cells, including absorptive enterocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) or chromogranin A+enteroendocrine cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), in the gut.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NIC-induced decrease in the number of chromogranin A+enteroendocrine cells in the gut.
source: Histological analyses of the small intestine in C57BL/6 mice treated with 200 μg/ml NIC (which emulates active smoking) revealed that NIC exposure decreased villus length without affecting crypt size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which was consistent with NIC-induced decrease in the number of differentiated cells, including absorptive enterocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) or chromogranin A+enteroendocrine cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), in the gut.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NIC exposure increased abundance of Ki67-positive cells in the small and large intestine.
source: NIC exposure increased abundance of Ki67-positive cells in the small and large intestine (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The number of proliferative olfactomedin-4 (Olfm4)-positive ISCs significantly increased in the small intestine of NIC-treated mice.
source: Consistently, the number of proliferative olfactomedin-4 (Olfm4)-positive ISCs significantly increased in the small intestine of NIC-treated mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of LgR5 +colonic stem cells (CSCs) was increased in NIC-treated Lgr5-EGFP-IRES-CreERT2 mice expressing EGFP under the control of the LgR5 promoter.
source: Moreover, the number of LgR5 +colonic stem cells (CSCs) was increased in NIC-treated Lgr5-EGFP-IRES-CreERT2 mice expressing EGFP under the control of the LgR5 promoter (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: We did not observe any changes in the number of Paneth cells in NIC-treated mice.
source: However, we did not observe any changes in the number of Paneth cells in NIC-treated mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The self-renewal of ISCs in NIC-treated mice increased with a reciprocal decrease in the number of differentiated cells.
source: These results indicate that the self-renewal of ISCs in NIC-treated mice increased with a reciprocal decrease in the number of differentiated cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A range of nicotine concentrations (100 nM, 1 µM, and 10 µM) promoted the organoid formation from crypts from the small intestine.
source: Our ISC proliferation analysis using intestinal crypts of wild-type mice revealed that a range of nicotine concentrations (100 nM, 1 µM, and 10 µM) promoted the organoid formation from crypts from the small intestine (Figure 2A), which was consistent with the in vivo data (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The same dose of cotinine, a minor tobacco alkaloid, and a major metabolite of NIC did not exhibit similar effects.
source: However, the same dose of cotinine, a minor tobacco alkaloid, and a major metabolite of NIC (Tan et al., 2021) did not exhibit similar effects (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 2A and a citation to Tan et al., 2021.

claim: The addition of 1 µM NIC promoted the organoid formation from colonic crypts.
source: Furthermore, the addition of 1 µM NIC promoted the organoid formation from colonic crypts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lgr5-positive ISCs isolated from NIC mice formed more organoid colonies than those isolated from control mice when cultured with or without Paneth cells.
source: Lgr5-positive ISCs isolated from NIC mice formed more organoid colonies than those isolated from control mice when cultured with or without Paneth cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-culture organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The addition of 1 µM NIC to control ISCs stimulated the organoid colony formation.
source: Consistently, the addition of 1 µM NIC to control ISCs stimulated the organoid colony formation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Paneth cells exhibited no significant difference in function (organoid formation) between control and NIC-treated groups, with or without CHIR99021.
source: However, Paneth cells exhibited no significant difference in function (organoid formation) between control and NIC-treated groups, with or without CHIR99021 (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: NIC directly stimulates ISC proliferation without affecting the supportive function of Paneth cell for ISC.
source: Therefore, this ex vivo assay for ISC function and ISC–Paneth cell interaction demonstrated that NIC directly stimulates ISC proliferation without affecting the supportive function of Paneth cell for ISC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the organoid formation assay data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Mecamylamine treatment completely abolishes the NIC-mediated formation of ISC-derived organoids.
source: We validated the significance of nAChR signal transduction using ISCs, isolated wild-type mice cultured in the presence of NIC, and the nonselective nAChR antagonist Mecamylamine, which indicated that Mecamylamine treatment completely abolishes the NIC-mediated formation of ISC-derived organoids (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Adiphenine exhibited no effect on the NIC-induced organoid formation from ISCs.
source: However, Adiphenine exhibited no effect on the NIC-induced organoid formation from ISCs, indicating that the effect of NIC was not mediated by these nAChRs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of NIC was not mediated by nAChR (α1, α3β4, α4β2, and α4β4).
source: However, Adiphenine exhibited no effect on the NIC-induced organoid formation from ISCs, indicating that the effect of NIC was not mediated by these nAChRs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of Adiphenine shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The existence of α7-nAChR in ISCs was detected by immunoblotting and RT-PCR.
source: The existence of α7-nAChR in ISCs was detected by immunoblotting and RT-PCR, respectively (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The higher expression of α7 and α9 subunits in both ISCs and Paneth cells were observed compared with other nAChR subunits.
source: The higher expression of α7 and α9 subunits in both ISCs and Paneth cells were observed compared with other nAChR subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There were no significant difference in expression of α7 or α9 subunit between ISCs and Paneth cells.
source: However, there were no significant difference in expression of α7 or α9 subunit between ISCs and Paneth cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The expression of human α7 subunit (CHRNA7) is higher than that of other subunits in both ISCs and Paneth cells.
source: In consistent with mouse data (Figure 3C), the expression of human α7 subunit (CHRNA7) is higher than that of other subunits in both ISCs and Paneth cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although the predominance of the expression in ISCs or Paneth cells was not clear (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: NIC treatment significantly upregulated α7-nAChR in ISCs rather than Paneth cells.
source: Interestingly, NIC treatment significantly upregulated α7-nAChR in ISCs rather than Paneth cells (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: NIC treatment did not induce other nAChR subunits in ISCs.
source: Importantly NIC treatment did not induce other nAChR subunits in ISCs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Addition of the α7-selective nAChR agonist PNU282987 increased organoid colony formation from ISCs.
source: Moreover, addition of the α7-selective nAChR agonist PNU282987 increased organoid colony formation from ISCs (Figure 3E), which was consistent with the effects of NIC.
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: α-Bungarotoxin, an α7-selective nAChR antagonist, completely inhibited the NIC-induced increase in organoid formation.
source: Furthermore, α-Bungarotoxin, an α7-selective nAChR antagonist, completely inhibited the NIC-induced increase in organoid formation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The effect of nicotine is mediated via the α7 subunits of nAChR.
source: These outcomes indicate the effect of nicotine is mediated via the α7 subunits of nAChR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: H89 dihydrochloride did not suppress NIC-induced organoid formation.
source: H89 dihydrochloride did not suppress NIC-induced organoid formation, however, Gö 6983 completely abolished this effect of NIC (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Gö 6983 completely abolished the effect of NIC on organoid formation.
source: H89 dihydrochloride did not suppress NIC-induced organoid formation, however, Gö 6983 completely abolished this effect of NIC (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The observed results with Gö 6983 was reproduced by Sotrastaurin treatment.
source: The observed results with Gö 6983 was reproduced by Sotrastaurin treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating other PKCs than PKCζ mediates the effect of NIC.
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Other PKCs than PKCζ mediates the effect of NIC.
source: The observed results with Gö 6983 was reproduced by Sotrastaurin treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating other PKCs than PKCζ mediates the effect of NIC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The PKC activator Ingenol-3-angelate stimulated the formation of organoid colonies from ISCs.
source: Consistently, the PKC activator Ingenol-3-angelate stimulated the formation of organoid colonies from ISCs (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: NIC does not induce PI3K/AKT signaling, p38/MAPK signaling, and mTORC1 signaling.
source: Results indicate that NIC does not induce these cascades and these were not required for the effects of NIC on ISCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting and organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: PI3K/AKT signaling, p38/MAPK signaling, and mTORC1 signaling were not required for the effects of NIC on ISCs.
source: Results indicate that NIC does not induce these cascades and these were not required for the effects of NIC on ISCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: YAP/TAZ, the downstream effectors of the Hippo signaling pathway, and Notch receptor 1 (Notch1)/Delta-Like protein 1(Dll1),the main components of Notch signaling are reported to be upregulated in NIC-treated organoids.
source: YAP/TAZ, the downstream effectors of the Hippo signaling pathway, and Notch receptor 1 (Notch1)/Delta-Like protein 1(Dll1),the main components of Notch signaling are reported to be upregulated in NIC-treated organoids (Takahashi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takahashi et al., 2018.

claim: Both the Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling pathways regulate intestinal homeostasis via the control of ISC function.
source: Both the Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling pathways regulate intestinal homeostasis via the control of ISC function (Mo et al., 2014; Sancho et al., 2015) and Notch signaling is positively regulated by YAP/TAZ in the intestine (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mo et al., 2014 and Sancho et al., 2015.

claim: Notch signaling is positively regulated by YAP/TAZ in the intestine.
source: Both the Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling pathways regulate intestinal homeostasis via the control of ISC function (Mo et al., 2014; Sancho et al., 2015) and Notch signaling is positively regulated by YAP/TAZ in the intestine (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2011.

claim: YAP1 and TAZ expression was significantly induced in the crypts of NIC-treated mice.
source: YAP1 and TAZ expression was significantly induced in the crypts of NIC-treated mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: YAP1 and TAZ also upregulated at mRNA level in ISCs from NIC mice.
source: YAP1 and TAZ also upregulated at mRNA level in ISCs from NIC mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Activation of Notch signaling in crypts of NIC-treated mice was confirmed through immunoblotting assay.
source: Moreover, activation of Notch signaling in crypts of NIC-treated mice was confirmed through immunoblotting assay (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The expression of genes, including Jagged1, HeyL, Hes1, Hes5, and Dll1, involved in Notch signaling, significantly increased in ISCs obtained from NIC-treated mice.
source: The expression of genes, including Jagged1, HeyL, Hes1, Hes5, and Dll1, involved in Notch signaling, significantly increased in ISCs obtained from NIC-treated mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling were not significantly activated in Paneth cells.
source: Notably, Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling were not significantly activated in Paneth cells, indicating that NIC affects α7-nAchR of ISCs rather than Paneth cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NIC affects α7-nAchR of ISCs rather than Paneth cells.
source: Notably, Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling were not significantly activated in Paneth cells, indicating that NIC affects α7-nAchR of ISCs rather than Paneth cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential activation of signaling pathways shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NIC induces a Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signal pathway in ISCs via activation of α7-nAchR and PKC.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that NIC induces a Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signal pathway in ISCs via activation of α7-nAchR and PKC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Treatment with K-975 and MK-0752 completely abolished the NIC-induced increased organoid formation.
source: Treatment with K-975 and MK-0752 completely abolished the NIC-induced increased organoid formation (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: K-975 or MK-0752 prevented the increase in the organoid formation in ISCs treated with PNU 298987 or Ingenol-3-angelate.
source: Furthermore, K-975 or MK-0752 prevented the increase in the organoid formation in ISCs treated with PNU 298987 or Ingenol-3-angelate (Figure 5C–F), suggesting that YAP/Notch signaling acts downstream of α7-nAchR or PKC leading to the response of ISC to NIC (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation assay data shown in Figure 5C–F.

claim: YAP/Notch signaling acts downstream of α7-nAchR or PKC leading to the response of ISC to NIC.
source: Furthermore, K-975 or MK-0752 prevented the increase in the organoid formation in ISCs treated with PNU 298987 or Ingenol-3-angelate (Figure 5C–F), suggesting that YAP/Notch signaling acts downstream of α7-nAchR or PKC leading to the response of ISC to NIC (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 5C–F.

claim: DBZ treatment significantly downregulated Hes5 protein expression in the crypts of NIC-treated mice.
source: We confirmed that DBZ treatment significantly downregulated Hes5 protein expression in the crypts of NIC-treated mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: DBZ suppressed the expression of YAP and TAZ in NIC-treated mice.
source: Notably, DBZ suppressed the expression of YAP and TAZ in NIC-treated mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the intestine, YAP/TAZ regulates Notch signaling.
source: In the intestine, YAP/TAZ regulates Notch signaling (Zhou et al., 2011) and Notch activation can activate YAP/TAZ (Totaro et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2011.

claim: Notch activation can activate YAP/TAZ.
source: In the intestine, YAP/TAZ regulates Notch signaling (Zhou et al., 2011) and Notch activation can activate YAP/TAZ (Totaro et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Totaro et al., 2018.

claim: Notch inhibitor suppresses YAP/TAZ and Notch activities, indicating a positive feedback loop between Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling in ISCs of NIC mice.
source: Consistent with previous reports, our results demonstrate that Notch inhibitor suppresses YAP/TAZ and Notch activities, indicating a positive feedback loop between Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling in ISCs of NIC mice (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 6B and previous reports.

claim: DBZ treatment did not alter the population of ISCs in the control mice but significantly suppressed the expansion of Ki67 +and Olfm4 + cells in NIC-treated mice.
source: DBZ treatment did not alter the population of ISCs in the control mice but significantly suppressed the expansion of Ki67 +and Olfm4 + cells in NIC-treated mice (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: DBZ suppressed the expansion of Ki67 + cells and CSCs in the colon of NIC-treated mice.
source: Moreover, DBZ suppressed the expansion of Ki67 + cells and CSCs in the colon of NIC-treated mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling pathways are crucial for ISC expansion in NIC-treated mice analyzed in vivo.
source: These outcomes demonstrate that the Hippo-YAP/TAZ and Notch signaling pathways are crucial for ISC expansion in NIC-treated mice analyzed in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: ISCs are the potential origin of tumors.
source: As ISCs are the potential origin of tumors (Barker et al., 2009), we hypothesized that NIC-induced ISC expansion can promote tumor formation in a tumor-initiating background, such as Apc loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barker et al., 2009.

claim: NIC-induced ISC expansion can promote tumor formation in a tumor-initiating background, such as Apc loss.
source: As ISCs are the potential origin of tumors (Barker et al., 2009), we hypothesized that NIC-induced ISC expansion can promote tumor formation in a tumor-initiating background, such as Apc loss.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested in the subsequent experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: A marked increase in the abundance of polyps was detected throughout the intestine of NIC-treated Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice.
source: A marked increase in the abundance of polyps was detected throughout the intestine of NIC-treated Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice; moreover, these polyps were significantly larger than that in the control mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by macroscopic quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Polyps in NIC-treated Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice were significantly larger than that in the control mice.
source: A marked increase in the abundance of polyps was detected throughout the intestine of NIC-treated Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice; moreover, these polyps were significantly larger than that in the control mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by macroscopic quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The area of β-catenin-positive adenomatous lesions throughout the entire intestine significantly increased in NIC- Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice.
source: Consistently, the area of β-catenin-positive adenomatous lesions throughout the entire intestine significantly increased in NIC- Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: NIC increased the overall polyp burden in the intestines of Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice by increasing their size and number.
source: These results indicated that NIC increased the overall polyp burden in the intestines of Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl mice by increasing their size and number.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: DBZ treatment effectively reduced the abundance of polyps and β-catenin positive adenomatous lesions in NIC- Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl.
source: Notably, this treatment effectively reduced the abundance of polyps and β-catenin positive adenomatous lesions in NIC- Lgr5CreERT2 Apcfl/fl, indicating the efficiency of DBZ for the prevention and treatment of NIC-induced intestinal tumors (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by macroscopic quantification and immunostaining data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: DBZ is efficient for the prevention and treatment of NIC-induced intestinal tumors.
